extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers and policy analysts studying media, social media, protest politics, and censorship (political scientists, communication scholars, data scientists)
extracted.subtask_short: analyzing media bias in protest reporting
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical analysis of selection and description biases in how protests are reported on social media by news media and government accounts; includes data construction, matching procedure, variable definitions, regression modelling, robustness checks, and typology of reporting styles (episodic vs thematic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection bias (media selection biases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether and how protests in the CASM dataset were selected for coverage by news media or government Weibo accounts (i.e. probability a protest is reported and frequency of reporting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured with logistic regression (binary outcome: whether covered) and quasi-Poisson regression (count outcome: how many times covered). Models include event- and user-level covariates; province and year fixed effects are included; standard errors clustered at province level. Interpret selection as systematic differences in which protests are reported by different account types (news media vs government and subtypes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Description bias (media description biases)
rubrics_metrics.description: How the descriptions of the same protest differ between individuals and news media/government accounts along multiple characteristics (action form, sentiment, police presence, mention of the state).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For action form, use a multinomial logit to distinguish disruptive vs violent; for other dependent variables use linear regressions. Include protest-level fixed effects so stable protest-level variables (location, date, issue) are adjusted for. Compare coefficients across samples (news media vs government vs individuals) to assess magnitude and direction of description biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action form (peaceful / disruptive / violent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify protest events' action forms into categories such as peaceful, disruptive, and violent and use these as dependent and explanatory variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Action form is used both in selection models (predicting whether account types report) and in description-bias models (how accounts portray the same event). For description comparisons, use multinomial logit to separate disruptive and violent portrayals. Note empirical findings: government accounts shy away from reporting escalated (disruptive/violent) protests; news media did not systematically over-report disruptive protests in China as seen in some Western contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure of the tone or sentiment of posts describing a protest (used to compare positivity/negativity across individuals, news media, and government accounts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentiment is included as a dependent variable in description-bias models. Robustness check: apply an alternative open-source Chinese sentiment classifier (PaddlePaddle) to confirm findings. Interpret differences in sentiment as part of description bias (e.g., government reports are more positive than individuals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Police presence (mention of police)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a post mentions police presence at the protest (binary indicator used in analyses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used both as a protest characteristic (explanatory variable in selection models) and as an outcome (in description-bias regressions). Empirical pattern: presence of police increases probability of selection by news media; government descriptions are less likely to mention police than individuals' descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mention of the state / government
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the post mentions the state/government explicitly; used as a variable to capture sensitivity or politicization in descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an outcome in description-bias models and as an explanatory characteristic. Note that news media avoid reporting protests targeting the government (selection), while government accounts may report protests targeting the state but frame them to depoliticize/desensitize the issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event matching procedure (constructing mentions of protests)
rubrics_metrics.description: Match CASM-China protest events to Weibo posts using a search based on 50 protest-related words; human verification of matched events; excluded multi-location events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors used 50 protest-related search terms to extract posts from ~9.5 million Weibo posts and then matched to 530 verified protest events. They randomly sampled 30 unmatched CASM posts to check omission bias (found 10% not in 9.5M posts, mostly due to homophones/evading censorship). Discard protests with multiple locations. Use human verification of matched events and a Random Forest classifier for matched-post labelling (precision 0.89, recall 0.76).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time window for matching / sensitivity analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Define a temporal window around a CASM event for matching social-media posts (primary: one week), with sensitivity analyses using two, four, and eight weeks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary analyses used a one-week timeframe for matching posts; authors ran sensitivity analyses extending the window (2/4/8 weeks) which produced similar results, suggesting robustness to window choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regression modelling choices (fixed effects, clustering, model family)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of statistical models: logistic regression for binary coverage; quasi-Poisson regression for counts (to allow variance>mean); inclusion of province and year fixed effects; clustering standard errors at province level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quasi-Poisson chosen because it separately estimates variance parameter, relaxing Poisson mean=variance assumption. Cluster at province level; do not cluster at year level when few years exist to avoid finite-sample biases. Use two-way fixed effects (province and year) to adjust for stable unmeasured provincial characteristics and macro changes over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covariates and variable operationalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Event-level covariates (size [log], action form, issue categories, police presence, target, mention state, sentiment) and user-level covariates (number of posts [log], number of followers [log], number of followees [log], verification status, total posts at collection time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include these covariates in selection and description models. Examples of issue categories used: land grabs, unpaid wages, homeowners, fraud, environment, pension, taxi, medical, education, veteran. Interpret coefficients to assess which features increase selection or shape descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of missing data and sample composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis based on complete cases after dropping missing values; exclude protests with multiple locations and passerby posts as necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors drop missing values for model estimation; they also conducted an additional analysis removing passerby posts (identified by a short list of words) and report consistent results. Document sample sizes (e.g., N of protests/posts) and account-type counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing media subtypes (government news media, commercial media, self-media)
rubrics_metrics.description: Split news media accounts into three types and compare biases and selection patterns across them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate separate models for government news media, commercial media, and self-media (zimeiti). Interpret differences: government news media are more similar to government accounts (less likely to report disruptive/violent protests), self-media more similar to individuals (but less likely to mention police).

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodic vs thematic reporting (reporting style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify reporting style as episodic (detail-oriented, the five Ws: who/what/when/where) vs thematic (omits details, focuses on root causes, government response and policy framing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize by comparing frequencies/ranks of top 25 words used by individuals and by media/government accounts. Words like 'police', 'real-estate developers', 'protest banners' indicate episodic detail; words like 'court', 'situation', 'legal case', 'protect' indicate thematic/government framing. Use close-reading examples to illustrate differences; quantify via word-frequency rankings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness checks and sensitivity analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct sensitivity analyses to test robustness: vary time window (1/2/4/8 weeks), remove passerby posts, include number of issues per protest as control, use alternative sentiment classifier (PaddlePaddle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report that results were similar under these checks (e.g., time-window relaxations produced similar results; removing passerby posts yielded consistent outcomes; sentiment robustness confirmed with PaddlePaddle). Document details in appendices as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bootstrapping for coefficient comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Use bootstrap resampling (10,000 samples) to calculate p-values when comparing regression coefficients across two samples (e.g., government vs news media coefficients).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply bootstrap to test statistical significance of differences between sets of coefficients (e.g., to confirm that government description bias is greater than media's). Report bootstrapped p-values and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of protest-level fixed effects for description comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: When modelling how descriptions differ between actors for the same event, include protest-level fixed effects so any stable protest-level variables (location, date, issue) are effectively adjusted for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identification strategy isolates differences in portrayal conditional on the same protest, controlling for unobserved fixed characteristics of each protest. Use multinomial logit or linear regression with these fixed effects depending on outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Random Forest classifier for matched-post labelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply a Random Forest classifier to label matched posts; reported performance: precision 0.89, recall 0.76 via fivefold cross-validation on 2,990 human-labelled matched posts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use supervised learning to classify matched posts where human labels exist; report cross-validated precision/recall. Use classifier outputs alongside human verification to construct the matched dataset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and exclusion of passerby/eyewitness posts
rubrics_metrics.description: Define criteria to identify passerby/witness posts (presence of specific words: weiguan 围观, pangguan 旁观, luguo 路过, shangban lushang 上班路上) and optionally remove them to test robustness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors removed ~2.5% of posts identified as passerby posts and reran analyses to check consistency. Document the exact keyword list used for reproducibility.
